title: Kinematics and Dynamics
bigQuestion: How can a few rules about position, velocity and force predict the motion of anything from a dropped ball to a crashing car?

story.title: Slowing Gravity Down
story.kicker: Around 1604 Galileo could not time a falling stone with the clocks he had. So he built a ramp, and made gravity take its time.
paragraphs: Drop a stone from a tower and it hits the ground in about two seconds. In the early 1600s no clock could split two seconds into useful pieces. Galileo Galilei, teaching in Padua, wanted to know how a falling body speeds up. Does it gain speed in proportion to the distance it has fallen, or in proportion to the time? Nobody could say, because nobody could measure a fall in progress.

His answer was a trick that physicists still admire. He took a long wooden beam, cut a straight groove down its length, lined the groove with smooth parchment, and tilted one end up. A polished bronze ball rolled down the groove far more slowly than it would have fallen straight down. The ramp did not change the kind of motion; it only stretched it out so that it could be measured.

For a clock he used water. A large vessel with a thin pipe let water run into a cup while the ball rolled. When the ball reached a mark, he pinched the flow and weighed the water on a fine balance. More water meant more time. He later wrote that he repeated each run many times, and that two runs never differed by more than a tenth of a pulse beat.

The pattern in the numbers was clean. In two units of time the ball rolled four times as far as in one. In three units it rolled nine times as far. The distance grew with the square of the time. That is exactly what you get if the ball gains equal speed in each equal second, the motion we now call uniform acceleration.

Galileo had not measured gravity's value; that came later. But he had shown that falling is lawful, that its law can be written in numbers, and that a clever setup can bring a fast, invisible process within reach of a slow instrument. Every graph and equation in this chapter grows from that groove in a wooden beam.
story.think: Galileo could not slow down time, so he slowed down the motion. What other fast or hidden processes might a scientist stretch out, shrink down or slow down in order to measure them?

lessons.title: Scalars and Vectors
lessons.mainIdea: Some quantities need only a size, but displacement, velocity, acceleration and force also need a direction, and that direction changes the math.
reading: A cross-country runner finishes a 5 km race and ends up 300 m from where she started, because the course loops around a park. Two different numbers describe the same run. The 5 km is her *distance*, the total length of the path. The 300 m, together with the direction back to the start, is her *displacement*, the straight-line change in position. Distance is a *scalar*: a size with a unit and nothing more. Displacement is a *vector*: a size plus a direction.

Physics keeps the two kinds of quantity apart because they add differently. Walk 3 m east and then 4 m north. Your distance is 7 m, but your displacement is 5 m toward the northeast, the hypotenuse of a right triangle. Vectors are drawn as arrows. The length of the arrow shows the size, called the magnitude, and the arrow points in the direction. To add vectors you place them head to tail and draw a new arrow from the first tail to the last head.

A vector can also be split apart. A wind blowing from the southwest can be described as one part blowing east and one part blowing north. These pieces are called *components*, and they let you handle each direction with ordinary arithmetic. Most of this chapter uses that trick: break a problem into horizontal and vertical components, solve each one, then combine the answers.

Speed and velocity work the same way. Speed is a scalar, the rate at which distance grows. Velocity is a vector, the rate at which displacement changes. A car circling a track at a steady 30 m/s has constant speed but constantly changing velocity, because its direction keeps turning. That distinction sounds fussy, but it is the reason the car needs a force from the road to stay on the curve.

words.d: a quantity that has only a size, such as distance, speed, mass or time
a quantity that has both a size and a direction, such as displacement, velocity or force
the total length of the path an object travels
the straight-line change in position from start to finish, with its direction
the pieces of a vector along chosen directions, usually horizontal and vertical

look.title: Two Routes Across the Loop
look.text: Two students leave the same corner of Chicago's Loop. One walks 4 blocks north, then 3 blocks east. The other walks 3 blocks east, then 4 blocks north. Both walked 7 blocks. Both end up on the same corner, 5 blocks from the start in a straight line, if the blocks are square.
look.prompt: Which quantities were the same for both walkers, and which one would differ if the second student had instead walked 3 blocks west?

check.q: A hiker walks 6 km north and then 6 km south, back to the trailhead. What are her distance and displacement?
check.why: Distance counts the whole path, 12 km. Displacement is the change in position, and she ended where she started, so it is zero.

check.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
check.why: Velocity has a direction as well as a size. Mass, time and temperature have only a size, so they are scalars.

check.q: A boat moves 8 m east and then 6 m north. What is the magnitude of its displacement?
check.why: The two legs form a right triangle. The displacement is the hypotenuse: the square root of 64 plus 36, which is 10 m.

lessons.title: Reading Motion Graphs
lessons.mainIdea: On a position-time graph the slope is velocity; on a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the line is displacement.
reading: A Metra train pulls out of Union Station. For the first minute its position changes slowly, then faster, then at a steady rate. Plot its position against time and you get a curve that bends upward and then straightens into a line. That picture holds every fact about the trip. The *slope* of a position-time graph, rise over run, is the velocity. A steep line means fast, a flat line means stopped, and a line sloping downward means moving back toward the start.

A curved position-time graph means the velocity is changing, which is *acceleration*. Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, measured in meters per second per second, written m/s². If a car's velocity goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s, it gained 2 m/s every second, so its acceleration was 2 m/s². Slowing down is also acceleration, with the acceleration vector pointing opposite the motion. Physicists avoid the word deceleration because the sign already carries that information.

A velocity-time graph makes acceleration easy to see. Its slope is the acceleration, so a straight sloping line means constant acceleration and a horizontal line means constant velocity. This graph hides a second gift. The area between the line and the time axis equals the *displacement*. A car moving at 15 m/s for 4 s sweeps out a rectangle 15 high and 4 wide, so it moves 60 m. A triangle under a sloping line gives the displacement during steady speeding up.

The three graphs, position, velocity and acceleration, describe the same motion in three ways, and each one is the slope of the one above it. Learning to move between them is the core skill of kinematics, the study of how things move without asking why. Galileo's ramp data was a position-time table. Its distance grew with the square of time, which is exactly the curve produced by constant acceleration.

words.d: the steepness of a line on a graph, found by dividing the rise by the run
the rate at which velocity changes, in meters per second each second (m/s²)
the description of motion using position, velocity, acceleration and time, without asking about forces
the change in position, equal to the area under a velocity-time graph

look.title: How Far a Dropped Object Falls
look.cite: Computed from g = 9.8 m/s², air resistance ignored; standard reference value
look.prompt: How does the distance change when the time doubles from 2 s to 4 s? What does that pattern tell you about the shape of the position-time graph?

check.q: On a position-time graph, what does a horizontal line segment mean?
choices: The object is moving at constant velocity
check.why: A horizontal line has zero slope, and the slope of a position-time graph is velocity. Zero velocity means the object is at rest.

check.q: A velocity-time graph shows a straight line rising from 0 to 12 m/s over 6 s. What is the acceleration?
check.why: Acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph: 12 m/s divided by 6 s equals 2 m/s².

check.q: Using the same graph, how far did the object travel during those 6 s?
check.why: Displacement is the area under the line. The area of a triangle with base 6 s and height 12 m/s is one half of 72, which is 36 m.

lessons.title: Equations of Constant Acceleration
lessons.mainIdea: When acceleration is constant, four equations connect displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration and time, and any three known values give the rest.
reading: A pilot needs to know whether a runway is long enough. A driver needs to know how far a car travels while braking. Both questions have the same shape: the motion has constant acceleration, and some quantities are known while others are not. For that case, five quantities matter: initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time and displacement. The *kinematic equations* link them.

The first equation comes straight from the definition of acceleration. Final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time, or v = v0 + at. The second comes from the area under the velocity-time graph. Displacement equals initial velocity times time plus one half of acceleration times time squared, or d = v0 t + (1/2) a t². Notice the t squared. That is Galileo's rule, distance growing with the square of time, now written as algebra.

A third equation removes time entirely, which is useful when you know how far something moved but not how long it took. Final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus two times acceleration times displacement, or v² = v0² + 2ad. A car braking at 6 m/s² from 24 m/s stops in a distance of 24 squared over twice 6, which is 48 m. Double the starting speed and the stopping distance quadruples, because the speed is squared.

The most important use of these equations is *free fall*. Near Earth's surface every object dropped in a vacuum accelerates downward at about 9.8 m/s², a value written as g. Air resistance changes this for feathers and parachutes, but for a dense ball dropped a few meters it barely matters. A rock dropped from a bridge falls 4.9 m in the first second and about 44 m by the end of the third. Timing the splash is a way to measure a bridge's height.

words.d: the set of equations that relate displacement, velocity, acceleration and time when acceleration is constant
motion under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored, in which acceleration is about 9.8 m/s² downward
the velocity an object has at the start of the time interval being studied, often written v0
the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface, about 9.8 m/s²

look.title: Gravity on Other Worlds
look.prompt: A rock dropped from 10 m takes about 1.4 s to land on Earth. Use the pattern in d = (1/2) g t² to explain why it would take about 3.5 s on the Moon.

check.q: A cyclist accelerates from 4 m/s at 1.5 m/s² for 6 s. What is her final velocity?
check.why: Use v = v0 + at: 4 plus 1.5 times 6 equals 4 plus 9, which is 13 m/s.

check.q: A ball is dropped from rest. Ignoring air, how far has it fallen after 3 s?
check.why: With v0 = 0, d = (1/2) g t² = 0.5 times 9.8 times 9, which is 44.1 m.

check.q: If a car's braking distance from 20 m/s is 40 m, what is its braking distance from 40 m/s with the same braking acceleration?
check.why: In v² = v0² + 2ad the stopping distance grows with the square of the starting speed. Doubling the speed multiplies the distance by four: 160 m.

lessons.title: Projectiles
lessons.mainIdea: A thrown object moves at constant horizontal velocity while accelerating downward at g, and the two motions happen at the same time without affecting each other.
reading: Stand at the edge of a table and, at the same instant, drop one coin and flick a second coin sideways off the edge. Listen. They hit the floor together. The flicked coin traveled farther, but it did not take longer to fall. That small experiment holds the whole theory of projectiles. The horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Gravity pulls down and only down, so it has no effect on sideways speed.

A *projectile* is any object moving only under gravity once it has been launched: a thrown ball, a jumping frog, a stream of water from a hose. Split its velocity into components. Horizontally there is no force, so the horizontal velocity stays constant and horizontal distance is just speed times time. Vertically the object is in free fall. It slows as it rises, stops for an instant at the top, then speeds up on the way down, all at 9.8 m/s².

Putting the two together produces the curve called a *parabola*. The shape is symmetric if the launch and landing heights are equal: the time up equals the time down, and the landing speed equals the launch speed. The distance a projectile travels horizontally is its *range*. In a vacuum the range is greatest at a launch angle of 45 degrees, and any two angles that add to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60, give the same range.

Air changes the picture for real objects. A baseball at Wrigley Field feels air resistance, and on windy days the flags along the outfield tell fielders which way to shade. But the coin experiment still works, and so does the physics of a dropped package from a rescue plane: it keeps the plane's forward speed while it falls, so the pilot must release it well before reaching the target.

words.d: an object moving only under the influence of gravity after it has been launched
the symmetric curved path a projectile follows when air resistance is ignored
the horizontal distance a projectile travels before it lands
not affecting each other, as the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile do not

look.title: The Ball Off the Cliff
look.text: A ball rolls off a 20 m cliff at 5 m/s. Picture the snapshots taken every half second. Each snapshot is the same horizontal distance from the last, 2.5 m, but the vertical gaps grow: small at first, then larger and larger. The ball lands about 2 s after leaving the edge, roughly 10 m out from the base.
look.prompt: If the ball had rolled off at 10 m/s instead, which numbers in this picture would change and which would stay exactly the same?

check.q: A bullet is fired horizontally from a rifle at the same instant an identical bullet is dropped from the same height. Ignoring air, which hits the level ground first?
choices: They land at the same time
It depends on the rifle's speed
check.why: Both bullets start with zero vertical velocity and fall with the same acceleration g. Horizontal speed does not change the fall time.

check.q: At the highest point of its flight, what is true of a projectile thrown at an angle?
choices: Its vertical velocity is zero but its horizontal velocity is not
Its horizontal velocity is zero but its vertical velocity is not
check.why: Gravity has used up the upward velocity at the top, but nothing has changed the horizontal velocity. The acceleration is still g downward.

check.q: Ignoring air resistance, which pair of launch angles gives the same range on level ground?
check.why: Angles that add to 90 degrees give equal ranges. Only 25 and 65 sum to 90.

lessons.title: Circular Motion
lessons.mainIdea: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating toward the center, and some real force must supply that centripetal acceleration.
reading: Swing a ball on a string around your head and let go. The ball does not fly outward. It flies off along a straight line, tangent to the circle, in whatever direction it was moving at the instant of release. Nothing was pulling it outward. The string was pulling it inward the whole time, and that inward pull was the only reason it went in a circle.

Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity, and a change of velocity is an acceleration. An object moving at steady speed v around a circle of radius r has an acceleration of v² divided by r, always pointing toward the center. This is *centripetal* acceleration, from Latin for center-seeking. It grows with the square of the speed, so a curve taken twice as fast needs four times the inward acceleration.

Newton's second law says every acceleration needs a force, so something must push or pull toward the center. For a ball on a string it is tension. For a car on a flat curve it is friction from the road. For the Moon it is gravity. The term *centripetal force* is not a new kind of force; it is a job description filled by whichever real force is available. If that force cannot keep up, the object drifts outward along a tangent, which is what a skidding car does.

The feeling of being flung outward on a spinning ride comes from your body trying to go straight while the seat curves in under you. The same effect shows up on a lab turntable: a coin near the rim needs more friction to stay put than a coin near the center, because at the same rotation rate its speed is higher. The sharpest curves on Chicago's elevated tracks are marked with low speed limits for exactly this reason.

words.d: center-seeking; the direction of the acceleration of anything moving in a circle
the straight line that just touches a circle at one point; the direction an object leaves a circle if released
the net inward force, supplied by tension, friction, gravity or another real force, that keeps an object on a curved path
the distance from the center of a circle to its edge

look.title: Newton on Circular Motion
look.text: Newton argued that a body moving in a circle must be constantly drawn toward the center, because a body left to itself keeps moving in a straight line. He compared the Moon to a stone thrown so fast from a mountaintop that it never reaches the ground but keeps falling around the Earth.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687) and A Treatise of the System of the World, paraphrased
look.prompt: In what sense is the Moon falling? Why does it never land?

check.q: A car rounds a flat curve at constant speed. Which force provides the centripetal force?
choices: Friction between the tires and the road
check.why: On a flat road only friction can point sideways toward the center of the curve. Gravity points down, and there is no real outward force.

check.q: If a car takes the same curve at twice the speed, how does the required centripetal acceleration change?
check.why: Centripetal acceleration is v² / r. Doubling v multiplies v² by four.

check.q: A ball is whirled on a string and the string suddenly breaks. Which way does the ball move immediately after?
choices: Straight outward, away from the center
Along a straight line tangent to the circle
It keeps moving in the same circle
check.why: With no inward force, the ball continues in the straight-line direction it had at that instant, which is tangent to the circle.

lessons.title: Inertia and the First Law
lessons.mainIdea: An object keeps its velocity, whether zero or not, unless a net force acts on it; forces change motion rather than cause it.
reading: A hockey puck slides across ice and keeps going. The same puck on a carpet stops in a meter. For two thousand years the carpet seemed like the normal case: things stop unless you keep pushing, so motion must need a cause. Galileo saw it the other way. The puck on carpet stops because friction acts on it. Remove the friction and it would slide forever. Motion does not need a cause; changes in motion do.

Newton made that idea his *first law*. An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving at constant velocity, unless a *net force* acts on it. The net force is the vector sum of all the forces on an object. A book on a table has two forces on it, gravity down and the table pushing up, and they cancel. The net force is zero, so the book's velocity stays what it is, which is zero.

The property that resists changes in motion is *inertia*, and mass measures it. A bowling ball and a soccer ball can sit equally still, but try to push each one into motion and the difference is obvious. In a spacecraft, where nothing weighs anything, a large steel tool is still hard to start moving and hard to stop. Inertia belongs to mass, not to weight.

The first law explains the lurch you feel when a bus starts. Your body was at rest and it tries to stay at rest, so the seat back has to push you forward. When the bus brakes, your body keeps moving forward at the old speed until something stops it. That something is either a seat belt, or the dashboard. The last section of this chapter returns to that choice.

words.d: Newton's rule that an object's velocity stays constant unless a net force acts on it
the vector sum of all the forces acting on an object
the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion, measured by its mass
the state of an object whose net force is zero, so it stays at rest or moves at constant velocity

look.title: Newton's First Law, in His Own Words
look.text: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a right line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed thereon.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia, 1687, in Andrew Motte's English translation of 1729
look.prompt: A 'right line' means a straight line. Why did Newton include 'uniform motion in a right line' together with rest, instead of treating rest as special?

check.q: A spacecraft far from any planet shuts off its engines. What happens to its motion?
choices: It keeps moving at constant velocity
It speeds up because nothing holds it back
It begins to drift in circles
check.why: With no net force, the first law says the velocity does not change. Nothing is needed to keep it moving.

check.q: Which object has the most inertia?
choices: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 20 m/s
A 1 kg cat running at 5 m/s
check.why: Inertia is measured by mass alone. The 5 kg brick has the most mass, whether it is moving or not.

check.q: A book rests on a table. Why does it not accelerate even though gravity pulls it down?
choices: Gravity is too weak to move a book
The book has no inertia while at rest
Friction holds the book in place
The table pushes up with a force equal to gravity, so the net force is zero
check.why: The upward push of the table balances gravity. Net force zero means no acceleration, exactly as the first law predicts.

lessons.title: Force, Mass and the Second Law
lessons.mainIdea: Net force equals mass times acceleration: the same push accelerates a small mass more than a large one, and acceleration points the same way as the net force.
reading: Push an empty shopping cart and it leaps forward. Load it with forty pounds of groceries and the same push barely gets it rolling. Newton's *second law* says exactly how much difference the load makes. The acceleration of an object equals the net force on it divided by its mass, or a = F/m, more often written F = ma. Double the force and the acceleration doubles; double the mass and it halves.

The unit of force is the *newton*, symbol N. One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s². It is about the weight of a small apple. A 1,200 kg car accelerating at 3 m/s² needs a net force of 3,600 N from the road. The word net matters. Engines, friction and air drag all push on the car; only their combined vector sum shows up in F = ma.

The second law also links mass to *weight*, which are not the same thing. Mass is the amount of matter and its inertia, measured in kilograms, and it is the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in newtons, equal to mg. A 70 kg person weighs about 686 N on Earth and about 112 N on the Moon, where g is 1.6 m/s², yet has the same 70 kg of mass in both places.

The second law is a vector equation. The acceleration always points in the direction of the net force, not necessarily in the direction of motion. A ball thrown upward moves up while gravity, and therefore its acceleration, point down. That is why it slows. Every problem in the rest of this chapter follows one recipe: find all the forces, add them as vectors to get the net force, and divide by mass.

words.d: Newton's rule that net force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma
the unit of force; 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²
the force of gravity on an object, equal to its mass times g, measured in newtons
the amount of matter in an object and the measure of its inertia, in kilograms

look.title: Two Sleds on the Ice
look.text: On a frozen pond a student gives a 10 kg sled a steady push of 20 N for 2 s. Then she gives a 20 kg sled the same 20 N push for 2 s. Friction on the ice is small enough to ignore. She measures each sled's speed at the end of the push.
look.prompt: Predict the two accelerations and the two final speeds. Then explain what she would have to change to give the heavier sled the same final speed.

check.q: A net force of 12 N acts on a 4 kg object. What is its acceleration?
check.why: a = F/m = 12 N divided by 4 kg = 3 m/s².

check.q: An astronaut's mass is 80 kg on Earth. On the Moon, where g is about 1.6 m/s², what are her mass and weight?
check.why: Mass does not change with location. Weight is mg, which is 80 times 1.6, or 128 N, on the Moon.

check.q: Two forces act on a box: 30 N to the right and 10 N to the left. The box has a mass of 5 kg. What is its acceleration?
check.why: The net force is 30 minus 10, or 20 N to the right. Dividing by 5 kg gives 4 m/s² to the right.

lessons.title: Action, Reaction and Free-Body Diagrams
lessons.mainIdea: Forces come in pairs that act on different objects, and a free-body diagram that shows only the forces on one object is the tool for keeping that straight.
reading: Lean against a wall and the wall leans back on you. That is not a figure of speech. Newton's *third law* says that when object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force of equal size and opposite direction on A. The forces always come as a pair. You cannot push on something without being pushed back, and the two pushes are equal, no matter how different the objects are.

This leads to a famous puzzle. If a horse pulls a cart forward, and the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal force, how does anything move? The answer is that the two forces act on different objects. The forward pull acts on the cart and the backward pull acts on the horse. To know whether the cart accelerates, you add up only the forces on the cart: the horse's pull forward and friction backward. The pair forces never cancel, because they are never on the same object.

The tool for keeping this straight is a *free-body diagram*. Draw the object as a dot. Draw every force acting on that object as an arrow pointing away from the dot, labeled with its cause: gravity, the *normal force* from a surface, tension in a rope, friction, a push. Leave out the forces the object exerts on other things. Then add the arrows as vectors. The sum is the net force, and F = ma finishes the job.

A free-body diagram of a person standing in an elevator shows two forces: weight down and the floor's normal force up. If the elevator accelerates upward, the normal force must be larger than the weight, which is why you feel heavier. If the cable snapped, the normal force would drop to zero and you would feel weightless while both you and the elevator fell together. Astronauts on the space station feel that every minute of every day.

words.d: Newton's rule that forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on two different objects
a sketch of one object as a dot with arrows for every force acting on it
the push a surface exerts on an object resting on it, perpendicular to the surface
the pulling force carried along a rope, string or cable

look.title: Newton's Third Law
look.text: To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction: or the mutual actions of two bodies upon each other are always equal, and directed to contrary parts.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia, 1687, Andrew Motte's translation of 1729
look.prompt: Newton says the actions are 'of two bodies upon each other'. Why does that phrase rule out the idea that action and reaction cancel?

check.q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water with her hands. What is the reaction force?
choices: The water pushing forward on the swimmer
The water pushing backward on itself
check.why: The pair partner of the swimmer's push on the water is the water's push on the swimmer, equal in size and opposite in direction.

check.q: A book is pushed across a table at constant velocity. Which forces belong on its free-body diagram?
choices: Weight, normal force, the push, friction
Weight, the push, and the book's push on the table
Only the push, since the book is moving
Weight and the normal force only
check.why: All four forces act on the book. The book's push on the table acts on the table, so it stays off this diagram.

check.q: A person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward. Compared with when the elevator is at rest, the scale reads
check.why: For downward acceleration the net force must point down, so the upward normal force from the scale must be smaller than the weight.

lessons.title: Friction
lessons.mainIdea: Friction is a force between touching surfaces that opposes sliding, roughly proportional to the normal force, and static friction can be larger than kinetic friction.
reading: A heavy box sits on a floor. Push gently and nothing happens. Push harder and still nothing. Push harder still and the box suddenly breaks free, and now it takes less force to keep it moving than it took to start it. This everyday experience contains everything important about *friction*. Friction is the force between two touching surfaces that resists their sliding past each other.

While the box is still, *static friction* matches your push exactly, up to a limit. That limit equals a number called the coefficient of static friction times the normal force pressing the surfaces together. Once the box slides, *kinetic friction* takes over, and it is usually smaller, so the box lurches. Kinetic friction is roughly constant regardless of speed. Neither kind depends much on the area of contact, which surprises most people.

The *coefficient of friction*, written with the Greek letter mu, is a number with no unit that describes the pair of surfaces. Rubber on dry concrete has a coefficient near 1, which is why tires grip. Waxed skis on snow are near 0.1. Ice on ice is lower still. Wet leaves, oil and loose gravel all lower the coefficient between tire and road, which is the physics behind every slippery-when-wet sign.

Friction is not simply the enemy. Without it you could not walk, a car could not start or turn, and a nail would slide out of the wood. Engineers spend as much effort adding friction, with treads, textured floors and brake pads, as removing it with oil, ball bearings and smooth ice. The rule of thumb is that friction does what the situation demands, up to its limit, and problems begin when that limit is reached.

words.d: the force between touching surfaces that opposes sliding
friction that keeps a resting object from starting to slide; it adjusts up to a maximum
friction on an object that is already sliding, usually smaller than the maximum static friction
a unitless number describing how much friction a pair of surfaces produces for a given normal force

look.title: Approximate Coefficients of Kinetic Friction
look.cite: Typical textbook values, rounded; real values vary with conditions
look.prompt: A 1,000 kg car has a weight of about 9,800 N. Roughly how much friction force can its tires provide on dry concrete, and about how much on ice?

check.q: A box is at rest on a floor and a person pushes it with 50 N, but it does not move. What is the static friction force on the box?
check.why: Static friction matches the applied force until its limit is reached. The box is not moving, so friction is exactly 50 N.

check.q: Why does a sliding box often lurch forward as soon as it starts to move?
choices: Its inertia disappears once it moves
Air resistance drops when it moves
The normal force decreases while sliding
Kinetic friction is usually less than the maximum static friction
check.why: The push that just overcame static friction is now larger than the smaller kinetic friction, so there is a net forward force.

check.q: If the normal force on an object doubles, what happens to the maximum static friction?
check.why: Maximum friction equals the coefficient times the normal force, so it is proportional to the normal force.

lessons.title: Forces on an Incline
lessons.mainIdea: On a slope, gravity splits into a component along the surface that drives sliding and a component into the surface that sets the normal force and friction.
reading: A wheelchair ramp, a loading dock, a sledding hill, Galileo's groove: all are *inclines*, and all are solved the same way. Gravity pulls straight down, but the object can only move along the slope. So tilt your axes. Let one axis run along the surface and the other point perpendicular to it. Now the weight splits into two components, and each one has a clear job.

The component along the slope is mg times the sine of the angle. It is the part of gravity that tries to slide the object downhill. The component into the slope is mg times the cosine of the angle. The surface pushes back with a normal force equal to it, and friction depends on that normal force. On a flat floor the angle is zero, the sine is zero and nothing slides. On a vertical wall the sine is one and the full weight pulls down.

Galileo's ramp was gentle, so the sine was small and the ball's acceleration was a small fraction of g. That is precisely why it worked. Without friction, acceleration along a frictionless incline is g times the sine of the angle. At 30 degrees the sine is 0.5, so the acceleration is 4.9 m/s². Steeper ramps give larger accelerations, all the way to free fall at 90 degrees.

Friction adds a third arrow to the free-body diagram, pointing up the slope for an object sliding down. A box will stay put as long as the downhill component of gravity does not exceed the maximum static friction. Since both grow and shrink with the same mass, the mass cancels: the angle at which a box starts to slide depends only on the coefficient of friction. Road engineers use this in setting the grade of highway ramps and the banking of curves.

words.d: a flat surface tilted at an angle to the horizontal; a ramp or slope
the part of the weight that acts parallel to the surface, equal to mg times the sine of the angle
in a right triangle, the ratio of the side opposite an angle to the hypotenuse
tilting a road curve inward so that part of the normal force helps turn the car

look.title: The Sled That Will Not Start
look.text: A student sits on a sled at the top of a snowy slope in a Chicago park. Nothing happens. A friend raises the far end of the hill with a shovel, making the slope steeper, and the sled suddenly slides. When a heavier friend sits on the same sled at the original angle, it still does not slide.
look.prompt: Use the components of gravity and static friction to explain both observations, including why adding mass did not help.

check.q: A 10 kg crate rests on a frictionless ramp inclined at 30 degrees. What is its acceleration down the ramp?
check.why: Acceleration on a frictionless incline is g times the sine of the angle. Sine of 30 degrees is 0.5, so a = 4.9 m/s².

check.q: As a ramp is tilted from flat to steeper, what happens to the normal force on a box resting on it?
choices: It stays equal to the weight
It becomes larger than the weight
check.why: The normal force equals mg times the cosine of the angle, and cosine decreases as the angle grows.

check.q: Two boxes of different mass sit on the same rough ramp. Which one starts to slide first as the ramp is tilted?
choices: Whichever has the larger surface area
They start to slide at the same angle
check.why: Both the downhill component of gravity and the maximum friction are proportional to mass, so mass cancels. The slip angle depends only on the coefficient of friction.

lessons.title: The Physics of a Crash
lessons.mainIdea: In a collision the body keeps moving until a force stops it, and stretching the stopping distance and time is what a seat belt, air bag and crumple zone do to lower that force.
reading: A car traveling at 15 m/s, about 34 miles per hour, hits a wall. The car stops in a tenth of a second, its front end folding. A passenger without a seat belt does not stop, because nothing has pushed on her yet. Newton's first law carries her forward at 15 m/s across the space of the cabin until the windshield or dashboard applies the force the car did not. That second collision is the one that injures.

The size of that force follows from the kinematic equations and the second law. Stopping from 15 m/s over 0.01 m, the thickness of a hard surface's give, requires an acceleration of over 11,000 m/s², more than a thousand times g. Stopping over 0.5 m, the stretch of a seat belt and the crush of a crumple zone, requires about 225 m/s², roughly 23 g. Same speed, same passenger, same change in velocity. Fifty times less force.

Every safety device in a car is a way to make the stop take longer. The *crumple zone* folds so that the cabin decelerates over a greater distance. The *seat belt* stretches slightly and spreads the force across the strong bones of the hips and shoulder. The *air bag* inflates in a few hundredths of a second and then deflates while the head sinks into it, extending the stopping time still further. Together they trade a short, violent stop for a longer, gentler one.

Crash-test data have been the evidence behind decades of design changes. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports that lap and shoulder belts reduce the risk of death for front-seat occupants by roughly 45 percent in passenger cars. The physics is the same for a cyclist's helmet, a gymnast's mat and a ship's fender: spread the stop over more distance and time, and the force falls.

words.d: the front and rear parts of a car designed to fold in a crash so the cabin stops over a longer distance
a strap that applies the stopping force to the body over a longer time and across strong bones
a cushion that inflates in a crash to extend the stopping time of the head and chest
the distance over which a moving object is brought to rest; larger distance means smaller force

look.title: Egg Drop, Two Ways
look.text: Two identical eggs are dropped from 1 m. The first lands on a concrete floor and stops in about a millimeter; it breaks. The second lands in a thick foam pad and sinks 5 cm before stopping; it survives. Both eggs arrived at the same speed and both ended at rest, so both had the same change in velocity.
look.prompt: Roughly how many times larger was the average force on the first egg than on the second? Explain using stopping distance.

check.q: A car stops suddenly. Why does an unbelted passenger move forward relative to the car?
choices: A forward force from the crash pushes on the passenger
The passenger keeps moving at the original velocity until a force stops him
The seat pushes the passenger forward
Gravity pulls the passenger toward the front
check.why: Newton's first law: with no force yet acting on him, the passenger keeps his velocity while the car slows around him.

check.q: How does a crumple zone reduce the force on the people inside a car?
choices: It reduces the car's speed before the crash
It increases the distance and time over which the cabin stops
check.why: For the same change in velocity, a longer stopping distance means a smaller acceleration and therefore a smaller force.

check.q: Two passengers are stopped from the same speed, one over 0.02 m and one over 0.4 m. About how do the average forces compare?
choices: The 0.02 m stop needs about 20 times more force
The 0.4 m stop needs about 20 times more force
The forces are equal because the speed is the same
The 0.02 m stop needs about 400 times more force
check.why: From v² = 2ad, acceleration is inversely proportional to stopping distance. A distance 20 times shorter means about 20 times the force.

review.q: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track in 60 s. Which statement is correct?
choices: Her average speed is 6.7 m/s and her average velocity is zero
Her average speed and average velocity are both zero
review.why: She covered 400 m of distance in 60 s, but she finished where she started, so her displacement and average velocity are zero.

review.q: The slope of a velocity-time graph gives
review.why: Slope is the change in velocity per unit time, which is the definition of acceleration.

review.q: A stone is dropped from a bridge and hits the water 2.0 s later. Ignoring air, about how high is the bridge?
review.why: d = (1/2) g t² = 0.5 times 9.8 times 4, which is about 20 m.

review.q: A cannonball is fired horizontally from a cliff. Ignoring air, what happens to its horizontal velocity during the flight?
choices: It increases as the ball falls
It drops to zero at the top of the arc
review.why: No horizontal force acts on the ball, so by the first law its horizontal velocity does not change.

review.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. Which statement is true?
choices: It is accelerating toward Earth's center
review.why: Its direction is always changing, so it accelerates, and that centripetal acceleration points toward the center. Gravity is the only force.

review.q: A 2 kg cart and a 6 kg cart receive the same net force. The 2 kg cart's acceleration is
choices: one third that of the 6 kg cart
the same as the 6 kg cart's
nine times that of the 6 kg cart
three times that of the 6 kg cart
review.why: From a = F/m, the same force on one third the mass gives three times the acceleration.

review.q: A book rests on a table. The reaction force to the table's upward push on the book is
choices: the book pushing down on the table
the Earth pulling the book down
friction between the book and the table
review.why: Third-law pairs involve the same two objects with roles reversed. The partner of table-on-book is book-on-table. Weight is a separate force from Earth.

review.q: Which change would most reduce the force on a passenger during a crash from a given speed?
choices: Increasing the time over which the passenger stops
Removing the crumple zone to keep the cabin rigid
review.why: For a fixed change in velocity, a longer stopping time means smaller acceleration and smaller force. Seat belts, air bags and crumple zones all do this.
